topic.subject: social
topic.title: Socialism and the Russian Revolution
topic.scope: liberals, radicals, conservatives, socialism, February and October revolutions, Lenin, Bolsheviks, collectivisation

misconceptions.statement: Liberals in the 19th century were the same as modern-day liberals who support universal adult franchise.
misconceptions.why: Students project current political terminology onto historical contexts without accounting for the evolution of political labels.
misconceptions.fix: 19th-century liberals were wealthy property owners who opposed universal suffrage and believed only men with property should vote.

probe.question: Did 19th-century liberals support the right of every citizen to vote?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because liberals have always stood for equality and democratic rights.

misconceptions.statement: Socialism means that the government owns every single personal item, including clothes and shoes.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse the state control of means of production with the total abolition of private property.
misconceptions.fix: Socialism focuses on the social ownership of the means of production (factories, land) to ensure equitable distribution, not the seizure of personal belongings.

probe.question: Under a socialist system, would a person be allowed to own their own house or clothes?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the government would take everything away from individuals.

misconceptions.statement: The October Revolution was a spontaneous mass uprising of all Russian people against the Tsar.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks often frame revolutions as singular, unified events, ignoring the specific role of the Bolshevik party's tactical planning.
misconceptions.fix: The October Revolution was a planned coup d'état led by the Bolsheviks to seize power from the Provisional Government, not a general public revolt.

probe.question: Who was primarily responsible for the events of October 1917?
probe.wrong_answer: The entire Russian population rose up together to overthrow the Tsar.

misconceptions.statement: Collectivisation was a voluntary program where farmers happily pooled their land to help the nation.
misconceptions.why: Students often assume government policies are implemented through consensus rather than coercion.
misconceptions.fix: Collectivisation was a forced policy where the state seized land from peasants, leading to resistance and severe famine.

probe.question: How did the peasants react to the introduction of collective farms?
probe.wrong_answer: They willingly joined the farms because they wanted to support the socialist economy.
